docs.title: Phase 7: GitHub REST Target Deconstruction and Reference Resolution
docs.text:
# Parse GitHub URL to extract owner, repo, commit/branch, and path
    parsed_url = urlparse(repo_url)
    path_parts = parsed_url.path.strip("/").split("/")

    if len(path_parts) < 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid GitHub URL: {repo_url}")

    # Extract the basic components
    owner = path_parts[0]
    repo = path_parts[1]

    # Setup for GitHub API
    headers = {"Accept": "application/vnd.github.v3+json"}
    if token:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"token {token}"

    # ... [fetch_branches and check_tree helper definitions] ...

    # Check if URL contains a specific branch/commit
    if len(path_parts) > 3 and path_parts[2] == "tree":

        def join_parts(i):
            return "/".join(path_parts[i:])

        branches = fetch_branches(owner, repo)
        branch_names = (branch.get("name") for branch in branches)

        # Fetching branches was not successful
        if len(branches) == 0:
            return None

        # Check branch name
        relevant_path = join_parts(3)

        # Find a match with relevant path and get the branch name
        filter_gen = (name for name in branch_names if relevant_path.startswith(name))
        ref = next(filter_gen, None)

        # If match is not found, check for is it a tree
        if ref is None:
            tree = path_parts[3]
            ref = tree if check_tree(owner, repo, tree) else None

        # If it is neither a tree nor a branch name
        if ref is None:
            emit_raw("ERROR", "The given path does not match with any branch and any tree in the repository.\nPlease verify the path is exists.")
            return None

        # Combine all parts after the ref as the path
        part_index = 5 if "/" in ref else 4
        specific_path = join_parts(part_index) if part_index < len(path_parts) else ""
    else:
        # Don't put the ref param in query
        # and let Github decide default branch
        ref = None
        specific_path = ""
If the input URL targets an HTTPS GitHub resource, urlparse breaks down the URI path into individual segments. The engine validates that both owner and repo segments exist. When a /tree/ separator is detected, the engine determines whether the trailing segments refer to a branch name (which may contain slashes, such as feature/auth) or a direct Git tree/commit SHA. It queries fetch_branches() and matches path prefixes; if no branch matches, it verifies the SHA via check_tree(). It then extracts any remaining segments as the root subpath (specific_path).

If found with Base64 encoding, the payload is decoded and parsed into a pathspec.PathSpec instance. Traversal proceeds normally if this request times out or returns a 404.

docs.title: Phase 9: Recursive REST Content Crawling and Backoff Engine
docs.text:
def fetch_contents(path):
        """Fetch contents of the repository at a specific path and commit"""
        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}"
        params = {"ref": ref} if ref is not None else {}

        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and "rate limit exceeded" in response.text.lower():
            if not token:
                raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")
            reset_time = int(response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset", 0))
            wait_time = max(reset_time - time.time(), 0) + 1
            emit_raw("WARNING", f"Rate limit exceeded. Waiting for {wait_time:.0f} seconds...")
            time.sleep(wait_time)
            return fetch_contents(path)

        if response.status_code == 404:
            # ... [Handle 404 logging logic] ...
            return None

        if response.status_code != 200:
            emit_raw("ERROR", f"Error fetching {path}: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
            return None

        contents = response.json()
        if not isinstance(contents, list):
            contents = [contents]
        # ...
The internal worker fetch_contents recursively traverses repository directories via the GitHub Contents API. When it encounters HTTP status 403 or 429 indicating rate limits, it checks for an authentication token; unauthenticated requests fail fast with an exception, while authenticated requests calculate the wait window using the X-RateLimit-Reset header, sleep via time.sleep(), and resume execution. Single-item responses (returned when targeting a single file) are normalized into single-element lists.

docs.title: Phase 10: Remote Stream Retrieval and Base64 Fallback
docs.text:
for item in contents:
            item_path = item["path"]

            # Calculate relative path if requested
            if use_relative_paths and specific_path:
                if item_path.startswith(specific_path):
                    rel_path = item_path[len(specific_path) :].lstrip("/")
                else:
                    rel_path = item_path
            else:
                rel_path = item_path

            if item["type"] == "file":
                api_counters["entry"] += 1
                entry_num = api_counters["entry"]

                if not should_include_file(rel_path, item["name"], gitignore_spec=gitignore_spec):
                    api_counters["excluded"] += 1
                    emit("CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=rel_path)
                    continue

                file_size = item.get("size", 0)
                if file_size > max_file_size:
                    api_counters["size_limit"] += 1
                    api_skipped_size.append(rel_path)
                    size_kb = file_size / 1024
                    emit("CRAWL_FILE_SIZE_LIMIT", num=entry_num, path=rel_path, size=f"{size_kb:.0f}")
                    continue

                if item.get("download_url"):
                    file_url = item["download_url"]
                    file_response = requests.get(file_url, headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))
                    content_length = int(file_response.headers.get("content-length", 0))
                    if content_length > max_file_size:
                        api_counters["size_limit"] += 1
                        api_skipped_size.append(rel_path)
                        continue

                    if file_response.status_code == 200:
                        files[rel_path] = file_response.text
                        api_counters["processed"] += 1
                        emit("CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED", num=entry_num, path=rel_path)
                    else:
                        api_counters["non_text"] += 1
                        api_skipped_non_text.append(rel_path)
                        emit("CRAWL_FILE_HTTP_ERROR", num=entry_num, path=rel_path, status=file_response.status_code)
                else:
                    content_response = requests.get(item["url"], headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))
                    if content_response.status_code == 200:
                        content_data = content_response.json()
                        if content_data.get("encoding") == "base64" and "content" in content_data:
                            if len(content_data["content"]) * 0.75 > max_file_size:
                                api_counters["size_limit"] += 1
                                api_skipped_size.append(rel_path)
                                continue

                            file_content = base64.b64decode(content_data["content"]).decode("utf-8")
                            files[rel_path] = file_content
                            api_counters["processed"] += 1
                            emit("CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED", num=entry_num, path=rel_path)
            elif item["type"] == "dir":
                # ... [Directory exclusion validation and recursion] ...
                fetch_contents(item_path)
Each entry in the API response is checked for type (file or dir). For files, relative paths are resolved if use_relative_paths is enabled, and exclusions and file sizes are checked. File contents are downloaded using download_url (raw endpoint) when available, verifying size via the Content-Length header. If download_url is absent, the crawler falls back to querying the Git blob API URL, verifying the payload size against an estimated Base64 ratio (len * 0.75), and decoding the UTF-8 text. Subdirectories are checked against exclusion filters before recurring.

    # --- Summary ---

docs.title: should_include_file()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Function-scoped closure within crawl_github_files) Signature: def should_include_file(file_path: str, file_name: str, gitignore_spec=None) -> bool:

Description: Validates whether a specific file should be ingested based on configured inclusion patterns, parsed .gitignore rules, and exclusion patterns. Inclusion patterns match strictly against the file's basename, whereas .gitignore specifications and exclusion patterns evaluate the full relative path.

    def should_include_file(file_path: str, file_name: str, gitignore_spec=None) -> bool:
        """Determine if a file should be included based on patterns"""
        # If no include patterns are specified, include all files
        if not include_patterns:
            include_file = True
        else:
            # Check if file matches any include pattern
            include_file = any(fnmatch.fnmatch(file_name, pattern) for pattern in include_patterns)

        # Check gitignore if provided
        if include_file and gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(file_path):
            return False

        # If exclude patterns are specified, check if file should be excluded
        if exclude_patterns and include_file:
            # Exclude if file matches any exclude pattern
            exclude_file = any(fnmatch.fnmatch(file_path, pattern) for pattern in exclude_patterns)
            return not exclude_file

        return include_file
The helper implements a short-circuiting filter chain. It first checks include_patterns; if defined, the filename must match at least one pattern via fnmatch.fnmatch. If included, it then evaluates gitignore_spec.match_file(file_path); matching files are immediately rejected. Finally, if exclude_patterns are specified, the relative path is checked against each pattern. The file is accepted only if no exclusion rules match.

Parameters: * file_path (str): Relative file path from the repository root or search directory. * file_name (str): Basename of the file (e.g., main.py). * gitignore_spec (pathspec.PathSpec, optional): Compiled PathSpec instance representing active .gitignore rules. Defaults to None.

Returns: * bool: True if the file satisfies all inclusion and exclusion constraints; False otherwise.

Raises: * None.

Example: 

# Real call site inside crawl_github_files (SSH pipeline)
if not should_include_file(rel_path, filename, gitignore_spec=gitignore_spec):
    count_excluded += 1
    emit("CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=rel_path)
    continue

docs.title: fetch_branches()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Function-scoped closure within crawl_github_files) Signature: def fetch_branches(owner: str, repo: str) -> list[dict]:

Description: Queries the GitHub REST API (/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches) to fetch all active branches for a repository. This helper resolves whether intermediate path segments in a /tree/ URL correspond to a branch name (including hierarchical branch names with forward slashes).

    def fetch_branches(owner: str, repo: str):
        """Get branches of the repository"""

        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches"
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and not token:
            raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")

        if response.status_code == 404:
            if not token:
                emit_raw(
                    "ERROR",
                    "Error 404: Repository not found or is private.\n"
                    "If this is a private repository, please provide a valid GitHub token via the 'token' argument or set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable.",
                )
            else:
                emit_raw(
                    "ERROR",
                    "Error 404: Repository not found or insufficient permissions with the provided token.\n"
                    "Please verify the repository exists and the token has access to this repository.",
                )
            return []

        if response.status_code != 200:
            emit_raw("ERROR", f"Error fetching the branches of {owner}/{repo}: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
            return []

        return response.json()
The helper dispatches an HTTP GET request with a 30-second timeout. If it encounters a 403 or 429 status code and no token is configured, it raises an exception indicating that rate limits have been exhausted. For 404 responses, it logs context-specific error messages distinguishing between unauthenticated requests and missing/private repositories. On successful responses (HTTP 200), it returns the parsed JSON branch list; otherwise, it logs the status code and returns an empty list.

Parameters: * owner (str): GitHub account or organization name. * repo (str): GitHub repository name.

Returns: * list[dict]: Array of branch dictionaries containing metadata such as branch names and commit SHAs, or an empty list if retrieval fails.

Raises: * Exception: Raised if an unauthenticated request exceeds GitHub API rate limits.

Example: 

# Real call site inside crawl_github_files URL parsing block
branches = fetch_branches(owner, repo)
branch_names = (branch.get("name") for branch in branches)

# Fetching branches was not successful
if len(branches) == 0:
    return None

docs.title: check_tree()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Function-scoped closure within crawl_github_files) Signature: def check_tree(owner: str, repo: str, tree: str) -> bool:

Description: Validates whether a specific Git tree reference or commit SHA exists in the remote GitHub repository by querying the /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{tree} endpoint.

    def check_tree(owner: str, repo: str, tree: str):
        """Check the repository has the given tree"""

        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{tree}"
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=(30, 30))

        emit_raw("DEBUG", f"check_tree | ref='{tree}' for {owner}/{repo} -> exists={response.status_code == 200}", dest="LOG")

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and not token:
            raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")

        return response.status_code == 200
This helper verifies whether a URL segment following /tree/ points to a valid commit hash or Git tree object when it does not match known branch names. It issues an HTTP GET request using configured authentication headers, logs debug output to the designated logging channel, checks for rate-limit violations, and returns True if the server returns HTTP 200.

Parameters: * owner (str): GitHub account or organization name. * repo (str): GitHub repository name. * tree (str): Git tree SHA or commit reference to validate.

Returns: * bool: True if the tree object exists in the repository; False otherwise.

Raises: * Exception: Raised if the request is unauthenticated and hits a rate limit (403 or 429).

Example: 

# Real call site inside crawl_github_files branch/tree fallback logic
if ref is None:
    tree = path_parts[3]
    ref = tree if check_tree(owner, repo, tree) else None

docs.title: fetch_contents()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Recursive function-scoped closure within crawl_github_files) Signature: def fetch_contents(path: str) -> None:

Description: A recursive worker that traverses repository directories using the GitHub Contents API. It handles HTTP rate-limit delays, evaluates ignore and inclusion rules, downloads file blobs, and processes child subdirectories.

    def fetch_contents(path):
        """Fetch contents of the repository at a specific path and commit"""
        url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}"
        params = {"ref": ref} if ref is not None else {}

        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=(30, 30))

        if response.status_code in (403, 429) and "rate limit exceeded" in response.text.lower():
            if not token:
                raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")
            reset_time = int(response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset", 0))
            wait_time = max(reset_time - time.time(), 0) + 1
            emit_raw("WARNING", f"Rate limit exceeded. Waiting for {wait_time:.0f} seconds...")
            time.sleep(wait_time)
            return fetch_contents(path)

        if response.status_code == 404:
            # ... Error reporting ...
            return None

        if response.status_code != 200:
            emit_raw("ERROR", f"Error fetching {path}: {response.status_code} - {response.text}")
            return None

        contents = response.json()
        if not isinstance(contents, list):
            contents = [contents]

        for item in contents:
            item_path = item["path"]
            # ... Path calculation, file vs dir branch handling, content downloading ...
            if item["type"] == "dir":
                # ... Directory exclusion checks ...
                fetch_contents(item_path)

        return None
fetch_contents traverses remote directory trees via recursive API calls. If it encounters a rate limit, it extracts the X-RateLimit-Reset Unix epoch timestamp, pauses execution until that time passes, and retries the request. When handling items within a directory, it distinguishes between files and subdirectories: files are checked against pattern and size constraints before downloading, while subdirectories are filtered against .gitignore and exclude_patterns before recursing on item_path.

Parameters: * path (str): Repository-relative path to a target file or directory.

Returns: * None: Populates the outer files dictionary and updates api_counters in place via closure references.

Raises: * Exception: Raised if an unauthenticated request exceeds GitHub API rate limits.

Example: 

# Real call site kicking off traversal in crawl_github_files
fetch_contents(specific_path)

docs.text:
Structure of individual JSON objects returned by GitHub's /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path} API endpoint.

Field Type Description name str The file or directory name (e.g., "main.py"). path str Full path to the item relative to the repository root. type str Object classification; expected to be "file", "dir", "submodule", or "symlink". size int File size in bytes (reported as 0 for directories). download_url str | None Direct URL to fetch raw file contents, bypassing Base64 payload envelopes. url str GitHub API REST endpoint for fetching the item's metadata and Base64 content. encoding str | None Content encoding type (typically "base64" when retrieving blobs via the Contents API). content str | None Base64-encoded string content, often wrapped with newline characters.

docs.title: GitHub API Rate Limiting and Backoff
docs.text:
GitHub imposes strict rate limits on REST API interactions: 60 requests per hour for unauthenticated callers and 5,000 requests per hour for authenticated callers. The module handles these limits through a two-tiered strategy: 1. Unauthenticated Fast-Fail: If an HTTP 403 or 429 status code is encountered with a response body indicating "rate limit exceeded" and no token was supplied, the module raises an Exception explaining how to provide authentication credentials via CLI flags or the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable. 2. Authenticated Backoff: If an authenticated request encounters rate limits, fetch_contents parses the X-RateLimit-Reset HTTP header (a Unix epoch timestamp), computes the remaining sleep time (reset_time - time.time() + 1), logs a warning, and blocks execution via time.sleep(). Once the backoff period expires, it retries the request recursively:

if response.status_code in (403, 429) and "rate limit exceeded" in response.text.lower():
    if not token:
        raise Exception("GitHub API rate limit exceeded. Please provide a GitHub token using --token or GITHUB_TOKEN env var.")
    reset_time = int(response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Reset", 0))
    wait_time = max(reset_time - time.time(), 0) + 1
    emit_raw("WARNING", f"Rate limit exceeded. Waiting for {wait_time:.0f} seconds...")
    time.sleep(wait_time)
    return fetch_contents(path)

docs.title: Access Control and Missing Path Resolution (HTTP 404)
docs.text:
When querying remote repository contents, HTTP 404 responses can indicate an invalid subpath, an incorrect branch name, or a private repository accessed without adequate token permissions. The module checks these conditions to provide contextual error feedback: * If no token is configured, it warns that the repository may be private and suggests supplying credentials. * If querying the repository root on branch main fails, it suggests verifying whether the default branch is named master. * Otherwise, it reports that the requested subpath was not found or the provided token lacks read access:

if response.status_code == 404:
    if not token:
        emit_raw(
            "ERROR",
            "Error 404: Repository not found or is private.\n"
            "If this is a private repository, please provide a valid GitHub token via the 'token' argument or set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable.",
        )
    elif not path and ref == "main":
        emit_raw(
            "ERROR",
            "Error 404: Repository not found. Check if the default branch is not 'main'\n"
            "Try adding branch name to the request i.e. python main.py --repo https://github.com/username/repo/tree/master",
        )
    else:
        emit_raw(
            "ERROR",
            f"Error 404: Path '{path}' not found in repository or insufficient permissions with the provided token.\n"
            f"Please verify the token has access to this repository and the path exists.",
        )
    return None

docs.title: Non-Text and Binary File Isolation
docs.text: Ingesting binary formats (e.g., compiled binaries, images, bytecode) into an LLM analysis pipeline can cause prompt corruption and context overflows. The module isolates binary files using two defenses: 1. Local Filesystem Encapsulation: When reading files cloned via SSH, files are opened using the utf-8-sig codec. Any UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError is caught, incrementing count_non_text and logging the event via CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT. 2. REST Blob Stream Validation: For API responses, base64 payloads are decoded within a guarded try...except block, while unexpected or unparseable JSON structures increment api_counters["non_text"] and emit CRAWL_FILE_UNEXPECTED.

docs.title: Multi-Stage File Size Validation
docs.text: To prevent downloading massive assets, file sizes are checked at multiple stages: 1. API Metadata Inspection: File size is checked against item.get("size", 0) before initiating a download request. 2. HTTP Content-Length Inspection: When downloading raw files via download_url, the Content-Length header is checked before buffering the response body. 3. Base64 Payload Size Estimation: When decoding inline Base64 data, the unpacked size is estimated using len(content) * 0.75 before invoking base64.b64decode, skipping oversized blobs early.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
While crawl_github_files.py manages remote source code extraction via GitHub REST endpoints and shallow Git clones, crawl_local_files.py serves as the primary local ingestion engine within the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder architecture. It abstracts local filesystem discovery by exposing a unified ingestion contract that matches the output schema of the remote crawler. The module traverses physical directory hierarchies, dynamically discovers and enforces nested .gitignore boundaries, applies user-defined glob exclusion and inclusion rules, validates file payload sizes, and defensively reads text content into memory while isolating binary or corrupt artifacts.

Under the hood, the engine relies on a single-pass traversal orchestrated via Python's os.walk(). Rather than collecting all system paths and filtering post-traversal, crawl_local_files.py intercepts directory entries in-place. By mutating the mutable dirs slice provided by os.walk(), it prunes entire unneeded directory subtrees (such as virtual environments, build targets, and metadata folders) before descending into them. File qualification is governed by an evaluation chain where paths must sequentially clear hierarchical pathspec rules, user-supplied exclude patterns via fnmatch, include filters, and file size limits before being decoded using utf-8-sig.

All operational telemetry, filtering decisions, and ingestion summaries are dispatched through the centralized messaging system in output.py. The crawler emits structured progress events throughout traversal, tracking excluded paths, skipped binary files, and size-capped assets, culminating in a crawl summary report.

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_local_files(directory, include_patterns=None, exclude_patterns=None, max_file_size=None, use_relative_paths=True) -> dict:

Description: Crawls a specified local directory tree, loads root and nested .gitignore configurations, dynamically prunes directories matching exclusion parameters, filters individual files through glob and size criteria, safely ingests text contents, and dispatches detailed telemetry events to stdout and log channels.

Parameters: * directory (str): Absolute or relative filesystem path to the target directory. * include_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns (e.g., {"*.py", "*.ts"}). If supplied, only files matching at least one pattern are ingested. * exclude_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns (e.g., {"*.pyc", ".git/*"}). Paths matching any pattern are skipped. * max_file_size (int | None): Upper threshold in bytes. Files exceeding this limit are omitted from collection. * use_relative_paths (bool): When True (the default), dictionary keys represent relative paths calculated from directory; when False, full paths are retained.

Returns: * dict: A dictionary containing an extracted file map under the "files" key: {"files": {filepath: content}}.

Raises: * ValueError: If the target directory does not exist or fails filesystem directory validation.

docs.title: Phase 1: Input Validation and Metric Initialization
docs.text:
if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []
The routine verifies that the target path points to an accessible directory on disk. If os.path.isdir returns False, traversal aborts immediately by raising a ValueError. It then prepares the accumulator files_dict to store relative file paths and string contents, and initializes telemetry counters tracking entry sequencing, processed files, excluded paths, size violations, and non-text decode errors along with their respective tracking lists.

docs.title: Phase 2: Root Gitignore Resolution
docs.text:
# --- Gitignore specs: {abs_dir_path: pathspec} ---
    gitignore_specs = {}
    root_gi_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    if os.path.exists(root_gi_path):
        spec = _load_gitignore(root_gi_path)
        if spec:
            gitignore_specs[os.path.abspath(directory)] = spec
            emit("CRAWL_GITIGNORE_LOADED", path=root_gi_path)

    # Translated reason strings (looked up once)
    reason_excluded = get("CRAWL_REASON_EXCLUDED")
    reason_gitignore = get("CRAWL_REASON_GITIGNORE")
Before walking the directory tree, the crawler checks for a .gitignore file residing at the root level. If found, it delegates parsing to _load_gitignore() and registers the resulting PathSpec object mapped to the absolute root directory path within gitignore_specs. Telemetry confirms the load operation via emit("CRAWL_GITIGNORE_LOADED"), and localized reason strings for exclude and gitignore skips are cached from the translation engine via get() to prevent repeated lookups inside loop iterations.

docs.title: Phase 3: Directory Traversal and In-Place Pruning
docs.text:
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        abs_root = os.path.abspath(root)

        # Check for nested .gitignore in current directory (skip root, already loaded)
        if abs_root != os.path.abspath(directory):
            nested_gi = os.path.join(root, ".gitignore")
            if os.path.exists(nested_gi):
                spec = _load_gitignore(nested_gi)
                if spec:
                    gitignore_specs[abs_root] = spec

        # --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            abs_d = os.path.join(abs_root, d)
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(abs_d, directory)

            reason = None
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_d, is_dir=True):
                reason = reason_gitignore
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern.removesuffix("/*")
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = reason_excluded
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_DIR_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=dirpath_rel, reason=reason)

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()
The crawler initiates an os.walk() traversal. If the current directory contains a nested .gitignore distinct from the root, its rules are loaded into gitignore_specs mapped to abs_root. Directory candidates in dirs are evaluated against both the aggregated gitignore specifications (flagged with is_dir=True) and glob patterns stripped of trailing /* qualifiers. Excluded directory names are accumulated into excluded_dirs, and dirs is mutated in-place via dirs.remove(d) against a shallow copy, preventing os.walk() from descending into ignored directory trees.

docs.title: Phase 4: Candidate File Filtering
docs.text:
for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            abs_filepath = os.path.abspath(filepath)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore (all levels)
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_filepath):
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_INCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                    continue
For each file in the sorted directory list, absolute and relative paths are resolved. The candidate file passes through a three-stage gating mechanism: first against all active .gitignore rules in scope via _matches_any_gitignore(), second against user-specified glob exclusion rules via fnmatch.fnmatch(), and third against glob inclusion rules. Failing any gate increments count_excluded, emits a categorized event (CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE, CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED, or CRAWL_FILE_NOT_INCLUDED), and skips remaining processing for that entry.

docs.title: Phase 5: Size Verification and Content Ingestion
docs.text:
# Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_SIZE_LIMIT", num=entry_num, path=relpath, size=f"{size_kb:.0f}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_ERROR", num=entry_num, path=relpath, error=e)
If a file passes filtering, its size is checked using os.path.getsize(). If max_file_size is defined and exceeded, the path is tracked in skipped_size_limit and skipped. Surviving files are opened using the utf-8-sig codec to transparently strip any Byte Order Marks. If decoding fails (UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError) or an OS/file-system error occurs, the file is classified as non-text, added to skipped_non_text, and documented via CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT or CRAWL_FILE_ERROR. Successful reads insert the decoded content string into files_dict under the relative path key.

docs.title: Phase 6: Traversal Summary and Telemetry
docs.text:
# --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_HEADER")
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_TOTAL", count=total_fetched)
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_PROCESSED", count=count_processed)
    if count_excluded > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_EXCLUDED", count=count_excluded)
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_SIZE_LIMIT", count=count_size_limit)
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)
    if count_non_text > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_NON_TEXT", count=count_non_text)
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)

    return {"files": files_dict}
Upon completing traversal, aggregate statistics are calculated by summing processed, excluded, oversized, and non-text file entries. A structured summary report is dispatched through emit() calls, surfacing total entries seen, files accepted, items filtered, and enumerating oversized and non-text files. The assembled files_dict is returned wrapped in a dictionary under the "files" key.

Example: 

# Actual standalone execution block from utils/crawl_local_files.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from utils.output import emit_raw

    emit_raw("INFO", "--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
    files_data = crawl_local_files(
        "..",
        exclude_patterns={
            "*.pyc",
            "__pycache__/*",
            ".venv/*",
            ".git/*",
            "docs/*",
            "output/*",
        },
    )
    emit_raw("INFO", f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
    for path in files_data["files"]:
        emit_raw("INFO", f"  {path}")

docs.title: _load_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path) -> pathspec.PathSpec | None:

Description: Safely opens and reads a .gitignore file from the local filesystem using UTF-8-SIG encoding. It compiles the lines into a pathspec.PathSpec object configured with the Git-standard "gitwildmatch" pattern syntax. If file opening or syntax parsing fails due to missing permissions, disk corruption, or format anomalies, the function intercepts the exception, logs a warning message to the "LOG" channel via emit_raw(), and returns None to allow directory traversal to continue without crashing.

Parameters: * gitignore_path (str): Filesystem path to the .gitignore file to be compiled.

Returns: * pathspec.PathSpec | None: A compiled pattern specification instance if successful; None on any I/O or parsing failure.

Raises: * No exceptions are propagated. All exceptions are caught internally.

Example: 

# Implementation from utils/crawl_local_files.py
def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path):
    """Load a .gitignore file and return a PathSpec, or None on failure."""
    try:
        with open(gitignore_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            return pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", f.readlines())
    except Exception as e:
        emit_raw("WARNING", f"Failed to load .gitignore at {gitignore_path}: {e}", dest="LOG")
        return None
Under the hood, _load_gitignore() guarantees resilient parsing of repository ignore rules. It uses utf-8-sig encoding to handle UTF-8 files with or without byte order marks, and passes the lines directly into pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", ...). If an I/O failure or permission error occurs, the exception is caught, formatted into a warning string, and dispatched to emit_raw targeting the "LOG" stream, returning None to prevent traversal failure.

docs.title: _matches_any_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_path, is_dir=False) -> bool:

Description: Evaluates whether an absolute filesystem path matches any active .gitignore specification in gitignore_specs. It computes the target's relative path against each specification's parent directory, skips rules where the path lies outside the specification's tree scope (indicated by leading ..), normalizes path separators to POSIX forward slashes, and appends a trailing slash for directory entries to ensure accurate matching against gitwildmatch directory rules.

Parameters: * gitignore_specs (dict[str, pathspec.PathSpec]): Mapping of absolute directory paths to their respective compiled PathSpec objects. * abs_path (str): Absolute filesystem path of the candidate file or directory. * is_dir (bool): Flag indicating whether abs_path represents a directory. Defaults to False.

Returns: * bool: True if the path matches at least one governing .gitignore rule; otherwise False.

Raises: * No exceptions are explicitly raised.

Example: 

# Implementation from utils/crawl_local_files.py
def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_path, is_dir=False):
    """Check if a path matches ANY loaded .gitignore spec."""
    for gi_dir, spec in gitignore_specs.items():
        rel = os.path.relpath(abs_path, gi_dir)
        # Skip if the path is not under this gitignore's scope
        if rel.startswith(".."):
            continue
        match_path = rel.replace("\\", "/")
        if is_dir:
            match_path = match_path.rstrip("/") + "/"
        if spec.match_file(match_path):
            return True
    return False
This helper enforces nested gitignore scoping. It iterates over each registered directory gi_dir and computes os.path.relpath(abs_path, gi_dir). If the relative path starts with .., the file or directory exists outside that .gitignore's hierarchy and is skipped. Cross-platform path separators (\) are normalized to forward slashes (/), and directories have a trailing slash appended (match_path.rstrip("/") + "/") to satisfy gitwildmatch directory matching conventions. The helper returns True as soon as spec.match_file(match_path) matches.

docs.title: Telemetry Counter Metrics
docs.text:
Internal state variables tracking traversal throughput and filter attrition.

Counter Variable Type Description entry_num int Monotonically increasing sequence number assigned to every evaluated file and directory. count_processed int Total count of files successfully read and stored in files_dict. count_excluded int Total count of files and directories excluded via .gitignore, exclude patterns, or include patterns. count_size_limit int Total count of files skipped because their size exceeded max_file_size. count_non_text int Total count of files skipped due to decode errors (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError) or OS I/O exceptions. skipped_size_limit list[str] List of relative file paths that exceeded max_file_size. skipped_non_text list[str] List of relative file paths that failed text decoding or file reading.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
crawl_local_files.py uses defensive error handling to prevent filesystem anomalies, permission issues, or binary files from aborting traversal runs:

  1. Root Directory Verification: The function validates the input path using os.path.isdir(directory). If the path does not exist or is not a directory, a ValueError is raised immediately, stopping execution before allocating crawler state.

  2. Graceful Gitignore Fallback: In _load_gitignore(), file opening and compilation operations are wrapped in a generic try...except Exception block. If a .gitignore file cannot be read (e.g., due to permission restrictions or encoding issues), the error is intercepted, logged to the persistent log stream via emit_raw("WARNING", ..., dest="LOG"), and None is returned. Traversal continues without the failed rules.

  3. Binary and Non-UTF-8 Artifact Isolation: When reading file content, crawl_local_files uses open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") inside a try...except block:

  4. UnicodeDecodeError and ValueError exceptions indicate binary data (e.g., images, binaries, bytecode) or non-UTF-8 encodings. These are caught, increment count_non_text, append the path to skipped_non_text, and trigger a CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT event.

  5. Other file system errors (PermissionError, OSError, or generic Exception) are caught in a separate branch, increment count_non_text, and trigger a CRAWL_FILE_ERROR event containing the exception details. Traversal then advances to the next file without failing.

  6. Relative Path Boundary Protection: In _matches_any_gitignore(), os.path.relpath(abs_path, gi_dir) computes paths relative to each loaded ignore specification. Paths containing leading .. are skipped via if rel.startswith(".."): continue, preventing rules in subdirectories from leaking into parent or sibling directories.

docs.title: exclude_patterns.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/exclude_patterns.py

Following the local filesystem traversal and boundary isolation mechanisms established in crawl_local_files.py, the exclude_patterns.py module defines the centralized inventory of default exclusion rules used across the entire repository ingestion pipeline. It provides a standardized set of glob patterns designed to filter out non-textual assets, dependency trees, compiler artifacts, temporary files, and environment metadata before source files reach downstream token profiling and LLM analysis components.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The exclude_patterns.py module acts as the authoritative filtering dictionary for both local filesystem ingestion via crawl_local_files.py and remote repository discovery via crawl_github_files.py. In automated codebase documentation architectures, unconstrained directory traversal poses severe operational hazards: injecting multi-megabyte binary blobs, minified vendor bundles, lockfiles containing thousands of repetitive entries, and compiler build caches into LLM context windows causes immediate token exhaustion, severe degradation of attention mechanisms, and runtime decoding failures. This module defines the baseline perimeter that restricts ingestion strictly to primary, human-authored source code.

Architecturally, the exclusion inventory is organized into seven distinct functional domains: static media and binary archives, build and distribution targets, environment directories and dependency trees, language-specific compiled artifacts, operating system and version control metadata, legacy IDE workspace configurations, and modern AI agent workspaces. The module defines patterns adhering to standard fnmatch glob syntax, distinguishing between directory-level subtrees (designated with a trailing /*) and leaf file patterns (designated with filename extensions or exact basenames). When ingested by crawler modules, directory patterns enable aggressive in-place directory pruning during os.walk() traversal, eliminating entire subtrees from disk traversal without inspecting individual child inodes.

The following diagram illustrates how the patterns declared in this module are evaluated within the ingestion pipeline to prune directories, discard non-relevant leaf files, and protect downstream inference components from context bloat:

docs.title: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS: set[str]

Description: A comprehensive set of string literals representing fnmatch-compatible glob patterns. These patterns identify directories, binary files, autogenerated lockfiles, environment configurations, and external tooling artifacts that must be omitted from codebase ingestion. The collection is segmented into seven logical categories, each targeting a specific class of non-source file artifact.

Parameters: * None (module-level constant).

Returns: * set[str]: A mutable set containing all 132 predefined glob pattern strings.

Raises: * No exceptions are raised during module import or set instantiation.

docs.title: Category 1: Media, Data, and Static Assets
docs.text:
DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS = {
    # 1. Media, Data, and Static Assets
    "assets/*",
    "data/*",
    "images/*",
    "public/*",
    "static/*",
    "temp/*",
    "tmp/*",
    "media/*",
    "*.jpg",
    "*.jpeg",
    "*.png",
    "*.gif",
    "*.ico",
    "*.svg",
    "*.webp",
    "*.mp4",
    "*.webm",
    "*.mov",
    "*.mp3",
    "*.wav",
    "*.pdf",
    "*.doc",
    "*.docx",
    "*.xls",
    "*.xlsx",
    "*.ppt",
    "*.pptx",
    "*.zip",
    "*.tar",
    "*.gz",
    "*.rar",

This partition targets static digital assets, compressed archives, binary documents, and generic asset storage directories. Media files such as raster images (*.png, *.jpg), vector assets (*.svg), video streams (*.mp4, *.mov), audio formats (*.wav, *.mp3), and proprietary document wrappers (*.pdf, *.docx, *.xlsx) contain no executable architecture or semantic source code. Ingesting these files into an LLM analysis pipeline consumes thousands of tokens per file in non-interpretable binary or base64 garbage, while risking decoding crashes. Directory globs such as assets/*, data/*, and public/* short-circuit traversal of frontend static resource repositories, while compressed archive extensions (*.zip, *.tar, *.gz) prevent attempts to parse packaged artifacts as plain text.

This partition filters compiled distribution directories, modern framework build outputs, diagnostic logs, and auxiliary test or legacy directories. Modern web meta-frameworks compile source code into massive intermediate client and server bundles inside .next/*, .nuxt/*, or .svelte-kit/*, while native and compiled languages produce artifacts in dist/*, build/*, target/*, bin/*, and obj/*. Including these generated outputs duplicates source logic across thousands of transpiled files, corrupting documentation generation with minified artifacts. Furthermore, testing suites (test/*, tests/*), documentation repositories (docs/*), and non-production pathways (legacy/*, deprecated/*, experimental/*) are intentionally excluded to restrict architectural mapping to active, production-grade application logic.

This section eliminates third-party dependencies, virtual environment runtimes, secret environment variables, and auto-generated dependency lockfiles. Third-party vendor trees such as node_modules/*, vendor/*, and Python virtual environments (venv/*, .venv/*) contain tens of thousands of external files that do not reflect the proprietary architecture of the host repository. Excluding .env and .env.* ensures sensitive production credentials, tokens, and secrets are strictly barred from being read or forwarded to external LLM providers. Lockfiles like package-lock.json, poetry.lock, and Cargo.lock consist of machine-generated dependency hash graphs that consume massive token budgets without providing high-level architectural insight.

This category isolates compiler-generated bytecode, language toolchain caches, test runner states, and compiled native binaries across multiple language ecosystems. In the Python domain, it excludes bytecode caches (__pycache__/*, *.pyc), linter caches (.ruff_cache/*), and test coverage instrumentation (.coverage, htmlcov/*). In JVM ecosystems, it strips intermediate class files (*.class) and packaged Java archives (*.jar, *.war). For compiled C, C++, and Rust ecosystems, native object files (*.o, *.obj), dynamically linked libraries (*.so, *.dylib, *.dll), and executables (*.exe) are pruned to avoid binary ingestion. Mobile toolchain dependencies and build outputs (ios/Pods/*, android/.gradle/*) are likewise prevented from polluting root directory crawls.

docs.title: Category 5: Operating System and Version Control Metadata
docs.text:
# 5. OS & Version Control
    ".git/*",
    ".github/*",
    ".svn/*",
    ".hg/*",
    ".DS_Store",
    "Thumbs.db",
    "desktop.ini",

This partition safeguards against descending into underlying version control metadata databases and operating system desktop management files. Version control repositories like .git/*, .svn/*, and .hg/* maintain compressed object databases, packfiles, commit trees, and staging indices that can cause recursive traversal loops or corrupt UTF-8 text readers. The .github/* directory, while text-based, typically houses CI/CD workflows and automated issue templates that fall outside internal codebase implementation semantics. Desktop index files generated by macOS (.DS_Store) and Windows (Thumbs.db, desktop.ini) are binary artifacts created automatically by file managers and contain no source information.

docs.title: Category 6: Classic Integrated Development Environments (IDEs)
docs.text:
# 6. Classic IDEs
    ".vscode/*",
    ".idea/*",
    "*.iml",
    ".eclipse/*",
    ".settings/*",
    ".classpath",
    ".project",
    ".vs/*",

This partition prunes user-specific and workspace-specific configuration trees generated by traditional integrated development environments. Directories like .vscode/*, .idea/*, .eclipse/*, and .vs/* contain localized IDE configuration state, window layouts, debugger launch hooks, and developer personal preferences. Project metadata files such as *.iml, .classpath, and .project represent internal IDE build paths rather than codebase architecture. Filtering these patterns ensures the resulting documentation represents the software project itself rather than the local toolchains of individual contributing engineers.

docs.title: Category 7: Modern AI Agents and AI-Assisted Tooling
docs.text:
# 7. AI Agents & Modern AI IDEs
    ".cursor/*",
    ".cursorrules",
    ".windsurf/*",
    ".windsurfrules",
    ".cline/*",
    ".clinerules",
    ".roo/*",
    ".roorules",
    ".agent/*",
    ".agents/*",
    ".continue/*",
    ".aide/*",
    ".gemini/*",
    ".antigravity/*",
    ".claude/*",
    ".copilot/*",
}

This section filters configuration files, memory databases, rule definitions, and cached workspaces generated by modern AI coding agents and IDE extensions. Tools such as Cursor (.cursor/*, .cursorrules), Windsurf (.windsurf/*, .windsurfrules), Cline (.cline/*, .clinerules), Roo Code (.roo/*, .roorules), Continue (.continue/*), and assistant integrations (.claude/*, .copilot/*, .gemini/*) frequently store local scratchpads, session transcripts, index caches, and developer prompt instructions. Excluding these agent directories prevents circular context pollution—where previous LLM agent interactions or tool-specific metadata contaminate subsequent knowledge base generation.

Example:

docs.title: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS Storage Contract
docs.text:
The primary data structure declared in this module is DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS, configured as a standard Python set[str]. This set guarantees uniqueness among glob expressions and provides $O(1)$ amortized membership verification when verifying pattern existence.

Field Type Description DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS set[str] An un-ordered collection of 132 unique string literals representing Unix-style glob expressions used to exclude directories and files during traversal.

docs.title: Categorical Breakdown of Exclusion Patterns
docs.text:
The inventory contains 132 individual pattern rules across the 7 domains. The following table provides the operational breakdown, syntax classification, and rationale for each category:

Category Index Category Domain Pattern Count Syntax Variations Present Primary Objective Risk Avoidance 1 Media, Data, & Static Assets 32 directory/*, *.ext Prevent ingestion of images, video, audio, PDFs, and archive bundles. Context window saturation by binary encoding; UTF-8 decode exceptions. 2 Build, Distribution, & Caches 24 directory/*, prefix*/*, *.ext Strip transpiled outputs, compilation caches, logs, and legacy/test trees. Ingestion of minified/transpiled code; redundant documentation of test fixtures. 3 Environments & Dependencies 20 directory/*, filename, *.lock, .env* Exclude package managers, virtual environments, lockfiles, and secrets. Multi-thousand file traversal in package trees; leaking secret credentials. 4 Language-Specific Artifacts 25 directory/*, *.ext, path/directory/* Block compiled JVM, Python bytecode, C/C++ native binaries, and mobile builds. Binary corruption; token waste on compiler caches and linter outputs. 5 OS & Version Control Metadata 7 directory/*, filename Prevent traversal into VCS internals and OS desktop view configs. Ingestion of Git packfiles/objects; filesystem metadata noise. 6 Classic IDE Workspaces 8 directory/*, *.ext, filename Filter local developer workspace state, debug launch files, and IDE projects. Noise from developer-specific environments and local IDE paths. 7 Modern AI Agents & Tooling 16 directory/*, filename Block prompts, session histories, rules, and caches from AI coding tools. Self-referential prompt injection; circular knowledge contamination.

docs.title: Pattern Syntax Taxonomy
docs.text:
The string patterns in DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS fall into three distinct syntax shapes, dictating how consumers like crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py interpret each rule:

Syntax Type Pattern Structure Matching Semantics Crawler Action Example Directory Subtree Glob <path>/* or <prefix>*/* Evaluated against directory paths relative to the crawl root. Mutates the dirs list in os.walk() to prune the entire directory tree immediately. node_modules/*, output-test*/* Extension Wildcard *.<ext> Evaluated against the basename of each file candidate via fnmatch. Bypasses file reading and skips text decoding if the candidate ends with the extension. *.png, *.class, *.pyc, *.lock Exact Basename <name> or <prefix>.* Evaluated against the exact file basename or dotfile prefix. Skips specific configuration files, secrets, or desktop artifacts. .env, .env.*, .DS_Store, Thumbs.db

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Because utils/exclude_patterns.py is a declarative configuration module containing only literal constants, it introduces no dynamic control flow, runtime branches, or I/O calls that raise exceptions. However, the design and consumption of these patterns rely on specific error avoidance guarantees:

  • Exception-Free Import: The module relies exclusively on Python standard built-in data types (set, str). It executes no filesystem queries, network calls, or regex compilations during module import, guaranteeing zero initialization failures.
  • Separation from Regex Backtracking (ReDoS Immunity): The patterns are formulated for Python's standard fnmatch library rather than complex regular expression engines. fnmatch converts shell wildcards into simple POSIX-compliant patterns, completely eliminating the risk of catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) during high-throughput path evaluation.
  • Cross-Platform Separator Normalization: Because all directory patterns utilize the standard forward slash (/*), consumer modules on Windows environments must normalize path separators (converting \ to /) prior to running fnmatch. If un-normalized Windows backslashes are tested against assets/*, matching will fail silently, leading to accidental ingestion of excluded assets. Both crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py enforce this normalization before matching.
  • Boundary Guarding with Trailing /*: Directory patterns strictly append /*. This prevents accidental collisions between directory names and similarly named source files (for example, ensuring a pattern targeting a docs/* directory does not match a standalone file named docs.py).

docs.text:

  • crawl_github_files.py — Evaluates remote GitHub repository trees and shallow clone filesystems against these exclusion patterns.
  • files.py — Handles filesystem I/O operations and path resolution for files that successfully pass exclusion screening.
  • call_llm.py — Benefits directly from exclusion filtering by receiving clean, low-noise context windows free from binary or dependency clutter.
  • flow.py — The central workflow controller that triggers repository crawls governed by these exclusion definitions.
  • main.py — The CLI entry point that receives user-defined exclusion patterns and merges them with DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS.

docs.title: files.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/files.py

Following the filtering of excluded assets established in exclude_patterns.py, the codebase processing pipeline relies on structured representations of surviving files to drive downstream language model prompts. While modules like crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py manage raw ingestion and decoding, files.py provides pure functional transformations that organize and index in-memory file content.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The files.py module serves as the structural serialization and content extraction layer within the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder architecture. Its primary responsibility is converting unstructured collections of file paths and file contents into compact, machine-readable text and indexed lookups. By formalizing repository structures into deterministic trees and providing indexed random-access content retrieval, it ensures that downstream reasoning nodes in nodes.py (such as ContextRouter, IdentifyAbstractions, MapAbstractions, and CombineTutorial) can interact with codebases without overflowing LLM context windows or losing file-to-path context.

The module operates on a standard files_data collection—an ordered list of (path, content) 2-tuples assembled during codebase traversal. In build_directory_tree(), the module extracts directory hierarchies and associates each file with an integer index corresponding to its position in files_data. This indexing allows subsequent pipeline stages to instruct LLMs to reference, score, and select files solely by lightweight integer handles. When specific files are targeted for in-depth reasoning, get_content_for_indices() resolves those integer handles back into content mappings, formatting dictionary keys with metadata comments ("{i} # {path}") to reinforce spatial and structural grounding for the language model.

docs.title: build_directory_tree()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def build_directory_tree(files_data: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> str:

Description: Constructs a compact, deterministic string representation of the codebase hierarchy from a collection of (path, content) tuples. The function groups files by their parent directory and suffixes each leaf filename with its integer offset in the input list ((idx:{i})). This index-tagging scheme gives downstream LLMs structural awareness of the repository layout while establishing a unified coordinate system used by pipeline nodes in nodes.py to select files for deep inspection.

docs.title: Directory Grouping and Index Tagging
docs.text:
dir_files = defaultdict(list)
    for i, (path, _content) in enumerate(files_data):
        dirname = os.path.dirname(path) or "."
        basename = os.path.basename(path)
        dir_files[dirname].append(f"{basename} (idx:{i})")

The grouping phase initializes an in-memory defaultdict(list) and iterates across the files_data sequence. For each entry, os.path.dirname partitions the file path into a directory prefix, defaulting to "." for root-level files where dirname evaluates to an empty string. The corresponding filename is extracted via os.path.basename, appended with its sequential index marker (idx:{i}), and appended to the directory's list bucket. Ignoring file content during this pass ensures the structural tree is assembled with minimal computational overhead.

docs.title: Hierarchical Line Formatting and Sorting
docs.text:
lines = []
    for dirname in sorted(dir_files.keys()):
        lines.append(f"{dirname}/")
        lines.extend(f"  {fname}" for fname in sorted(dir_files[dirname]))
    return "\n".join(lines)

The formatting phase enforces strict lexicographical ordering on both the directory keys and the underlying file lists. Sorting directory names ensures deterministic output across different platforms and filesystem walk orders, which directly stabilizes prompt hash generation and enables effective prompt caching in call_llm.py. Directory headers are rendered with a trailing slash (/), and nested files are indented by two spaces (), resulting in an ultra-compact visual hierarchy delimited by standard newline characters.

Parameters: * files_data (list[tuple[str, str]]): Ordered collection of 2-tuples where index 0 is the relative POSIX file path and index 1 is the decoded text content.

Returns: * str: A multiline formatted string depicting the codebase directory tree, where each directory appears as dirname/ and each file appears indented as filename.ext (idx:N).

Raises: * No explicit exceptions are raised. Handles empty input gracefully by returning an empty string.

Example: 

# Extracted from source implementation in utils/files.py
def build_directory_tree(files_data):
    dir_files = defaultdict(list)
    for i, (path, _content) in enumerate(files_data):
        dirname = os.path.dirname(path) or "."
        basename = os.path.basename(path)
        dir_files[dirname].append(f"{basename} (idx:{i})")

    lines = []
    for dirname in sorted(dir_files.keys()):
        lines.append(f"{dirname}/")
        lines.extend(f"  {fname}" for fname in sorted(dir_files[dirname]))
    return "\n".join(lines)

docs.title: get_content_for_indices()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def get_content_for_indices(files_data: list[tuple[str, str]], indices: list[int] | set[int] | collections.abc.Iterable[int]) -> dict[str, str]:

Description: Resolves a subset of file contents from files_data by their numerical indices. For each valid index, it constructs a composite dictionary key pairing the index with the file path ("{i} # {path}"), mapping directly to the file's text content. This contextual key formatting guarantees that when the resulting dictionary is rendered as JSON or Markdown within LLM prompts, the language model retains explicit visibility over both the numerical handle and the semantic file path.

docs.title: Boundary Validation and Contextual Key Assembly
docs.text:
def get_content_for_indices(files_data, indices):
    """Get file content for specific indices from files_data list."""
    content_map = {}
    for i in indices:
        if 0 <= i < len(files_data):
            path, content = files_data[i]
            content_map[f"{i} # {path}"] = content  # Use index + path as key for context
    return content_map

The function iterates over the collection of requested integer indices and performs defensive boundary checks (0 <= i < len(files_data)). Any negative indices or indices that exceed the boundaries of the files_data list are silently bypassed, preventing IndexError exceptions if an LLM hallucinates out-of-range identifiers. For valid offsets, the (path, content) tuple is unpacked, and the dictionary key is formatted using an inline Python-style comment delimiter (#). This structure yields a self-documenting payload for prompt contexts that connects index references to filesystem paths.

Parameters: * files_data (list[tuple[str, str]]): Master list of codebase files represented as (path, content) tuples. * indices (Iterable[int]): An iterable of integer index references indicating which files to extract.

Returns: * dict[str, str]: A dictionary where keys follow the pattern "{index} # {relative_file_path}" and values contain the corresponding file content strings.

Raises: * No explicit exceptions are raised; invalid or out-of-bounds indices are discarded.

Example: 

# Extracted from source implementation in utils/files.py
def get_content_for_indices(files_data, indices):
    content_map = {}
    for i in indices:
        if 0 <= i < len(files_data):
            path, content = files_data[i]
            content_map[f"{i} # {path}"] = content
    return content_map

docs.title: FilesData
docs.text:
An ordered list representing the ingested codebase assets passed between workflow stages.

Field Type Description [i][0] str Relative file path normalized to POSIX style (e.g., src/core/engine.py). [i][1] str Complete decoded UTF-8 file content.

docs.title: IndexedContentMap
docs.text:
Dictionary generated by get_content_for_indices() providing targeted source content for LLM reasoning prompts.

Field Type Description Key str Context identifier formatted as "{index} # {filepath}" (e.g., "4 # src/utils/files.py"). Value str Raw UTF-8 source code content corresponding to the targeted file.

docs.title: DirectoryTreeString
docs.text:
A compact multiline string generated by build_directory_tree(). It uses indentation and index annotations to summarize the codebase hierarchy.

Component Format Pattern Example Directory Header "{dirname}/" utils/ or ./ File Item " {basename} (idx:{index})" files.py (idx:4)

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The functions in files.py apply defensive programming techniques to guarantee predictable execution when handling dynamic file structures and unstructured LLM outputs:

  • Directory Name Normalization: Root-level files have an empty directory component when processed by os.path.dirname(path). The expression os.path.dirname(path) or "." normalizes empty strings to ".", ensuring root files are grouped predictably rather than keyed under an empty string.
  • Deterministic Output Sorting: To maintain idempotent LLM prompt payloads across disparate operating systems, build_directory_tree() sorts both directory keys (sorted(dir_files.keys())) and child files (sorted(dir_files[dirname])). This prevents arbitrary filesystem iteration orders from busting prompt caches managed by call_llm.py.
  • Defensive Range Checking: In get_content_for_indices(), index bounds are validated using 0 <= i < len(files_data). If a downstream model hallucinates an invalid or negative integer index, the entry is dropped without raising an IndexError or halting the execution pipeline.

docs.text:

  • crawl_github_files.py — Remote repository crawler providing GitHub-based source inputs formatted as files_data.
  • exclude_patterns.py — Defines the pattern exclusion rules that filter code assets before files.py processes them.
  • nodes.py — Implements pipeline nodes (ContextRouter, IdentifyAbstractions, MapAbstractions, and CombineTutorial) that consume the directory trees and indexed contents generated by this module.
  • call_llm.py — Inference engine that benefits from the deterministic sorting of tree representations through prompt caching.

docs.title: i18n.py
docs.text: Source: utils/i18n.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
While utils/files.py structures and formats local source code repositories into serialized hierarchical representations for pipeline consumption, utils/i18n.py manages runtime UI localization and translation automation. The module provides dynamic internationalization facilities that detect untranslated UI and logging strings across execution phases, query large language models for bulk translation, and mutate the centralized localization ledger (strings.csv) in place.

Architecturally, this module was extracted from utils/output.py to decouple a problematic circular dependency chain: output.py $\rightarrow$ utils/call_llm.py $\rightarrow$ utils/token_utils.py $\rightarrow$ output.py. By isolating the translation workflow within utils/i18n.py, the system ensures that inference logic is only invoked on demand when missing string definitions are identified. The rest of the reporting infrastructure can emit messages without requiring premature loading of LLM client libraries or inference configurations.

The operational pipeline reads a UTF-8 with BOM (utf-8-sig) formatted CSV file, inspects header columns for target language coverage, compiles untranslated entries into a structured JSON payload, formats a prompt from an external Markdown template, and invokes the inference provider via utils/call_llm.py. Upon obtaining a valid model response, it uses defensive regular expressions to parse out the translated JSON dictionary, updates the CSV schema if a new language column is introduced, and writes the mutated records back to disk with BOM encoding intact.
